verdict.reasoning: The patient states, 'I keep having a headache,' and later confirms she has not really had headaches before, indicating a new-onset headache.
When asked when it started, the patient says, 'It started yesterday,' and later specifies, 'About mid-morning.'

Location and quality are described as, 'It's on the left side at the back, sort of here,' and 'just quite, intense, and kinda quite throbbing,' supporting a unilateral left posterior throbbing headache.
The transcript supports gradual onset: 'It kind of built up gradually after, over. A short period of time.' However, the patient never states that the headache is 'constant'; this is not documented.
In response to the 0–10 scale, the patient answers, 'I'd say about eight.'

The doctor asks about positional change: 'Any difference if you lie down, stand up, bend over, cough or sneeze, or anything like that?' The patient replies, 'Um, no,' indicating no change with posture.
The patient reports, 'I took some, um, um, Nurofen, yesterday,' and when asked if it made a difference, replies, 'Not really,' indicating ibuprofen with minimal relief.

The transcript supports no nausea/vomiting ('No, nothing like that'), no visual changes or photophobia ('No' to blurred vision and 'Any ... funny lights...?' 'No'), no neurological deficits ('Any nausea, vomiting, tingling, numbness, weakness, anywhere?' 'No, nothing.'), no fever/chills ('No, no fever'), and no rash ('No'). Neck stiffness and neurological symptoms as red-flag triggers are mentioned by the doctor but the patient is not asked or does not deny neck stiffness explicitly, so 'no neck stiffness reported' is an addition.

The patient denies current medical problems: 'have you got any other medical problems? ... no I haven't.' However, surgical history is never discussed, so stating 'no past surgical history' introduces new information.

'Any over-the-counter medications or allergies?' Patient: 'No, only the, Nurofen I took yesterday, Ibuprofen.' This documents a single recent use, not an as-needed pattern; describing it as a regular PRN use is not stated.
When asked, 'any over-the-counter medications or allergies?' the patient replies, 'No, only the, Nurofen I took yesterday,' implying she has no allergies to report.
Family history: 'my mother's had hypertension, and she does get migraines.'

She states, 'My partner' when asked who she lives with, 'I'm a designer' for job, and denies substances: 'do you smoke...?' 'No I don't.' 'Do you drink any alcohol regularly?' 'No.' 'any other drugs?' 'No.' She also answers changes: 'Is there anything you think's changed? Any increased stress, change in your diet or lifestyle?' 'Not that I can think of,' supporting no change in diet or stress.

The transcript supports an acute unilateral headache with no red flags (no fever, rash, vomiting, neurological deficits, or positional change). While 'tension versus migraine' and 'primary' are clinician inferences, they are reasonable direct clinical interpretations of the data and consistent with the doctor's reassurance and management plan.

The doctor says, 'trying a slightly stronger, pain relief. Uh, so, similar to Ibuprofen, but taking instead of Ibuprofen not at the same time... You can take Paracetamol along with that.' This means not to take the stronger NSAID together with ibuprofen, but paracetamol can be taken concurrently. The fact's phrase 'may alternate or stack with paracetamol' implies a general alternation/stacking strategy not clearly stated and omits the explicit instruction to avoid taking it with ibuprofen; overall it misrepresents the instruction regarding combination/alternation.
The doctor advises, 'Try and um, take rest, have lots of good hydration,' which matches encouraging rest and hydration.

The doctor states to call back 'if the pain's getting worse, or you get new symptoms, fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness... or you keep getting episodes of the same type of thing,' and later, 'if it's getting worse or not settling in the next day or two. Then certainly give us a call back.' This supports follow-up if worsening, persisting beyond ~48 hours, or if red-flag signs like fever, rash, vomiting, neck stiffness develop. Neurological symptoms are a reasonable direct inference from the red-flag context.
